Abstract

The subadditivity–doubling–rotation (SDR) technique is a powerful route to Gaussian optimality in classical information theory and relies on strict subadditivity and its equality-case analysis, where double Markovity is a standard tool. We establish quantum analogues of double Markovity. For tripartite states, we characterize the simultaneous Markov conditions A–B–C and A–C–B via compatible projective measurements on B and C that induce a common classical label J yielding A–J–(B,C). For strictly positive four-party states, we show that A–(B,D)–C and A–(C,D)–B hold if and only if A–D–(B,C) holds. These results remove a key bottleneck in extending SDR-type arguments to quantum systems.

I Introduction

Gaussian distributions play a distinguished role not only in classical information theory, but also in quantum information theory, where Gaussian extremality questions arise in a variety of entropy inequalities and optimization problems for quantum systems. A recurring theme—spanning functional inequalities and multi-terminal problems—is that extremizers of information-theoretic functionals under second-moment constraints are often Gaussian.

In the classical setting, a particularly robust route to Gaussian extremality is the subadditivity–doubling–rotation (SDR) proof paradigm. At the heart of SDR lies a strict form of subadditivity: one needs to identify when equality in a subadditivity inequality forces an independence (or conditional independence) structure. A widely used tool for establishing such equality conditions is the double Markovity property of Markov chains (cf. [1, Exercise 16.25]), which, informally, says that if AA is conditionally independent of CC given BB and also conditionally independent of BB given CC, then BB and CC must share a common “summary” variable that screens off AA.

Historically, the “doubling–rotation” idea originates in functional analysis: it appeared in Lieb’s work [2] on Gaussian kernels and in Carlen’s work [3] on Gaussian optimality for the log-Sobolev inequality. In information theory, it was brought to the forefront by Geng and Nair [4] in the study of Gaussian broadcast channels, where it was combined with subadditivity to establish Gaussian optimality. Since then, SDR-type arguments have been used to prove a number of information inequalities [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10], and their use in proving the entropy power inequality was developed in [11].

While quantum information theory has analogues of many classical inequalities, extending the SDR paradigm to quantum systems faces a conceptual bottleneck: an appropriate quantum counterpart of double Markovity has not been available in a form suitable for equality-case analysis. The purpose of this paper is to fill this gap by establishing two quantum versions of double Markovity that parallel the most commonly used classical formulations. These results remove an important obstacle in transporting the SDR methodology to quantum information-theoretic settings.

To formulate these quantum analogues precisely, we next recall the notion of a quantum Markov chain and state the corresponding “double Markovity” question in quantum terms. We work with finite-dimensional quantum systems A,B,C,…A,B,C,\ldots with Hilbert spaces ℋA,ℋB,ℋC,…\mathcal{H}_{A},\mathcal{H}_{B},\mathcal{H}_{C},\ldots. A (density) state on AA is a positive semidefinite operator ρA\rho_{A} with Tr⁡ρA=1\Tr\rho_{A}=1; for a composite system A​BAB we write ρA​B\rho_{AB} for a joint state and ρA=TrB⁡ρA​B\rho_{A}=\Tr_{B}\rho_{AB} for the marginal. To express Markov-type conditional independence in quantum terms, we use the conditional mutual information (CMI) defined from von Neumann entropies, which are defined as S⁡(A):=S⁡(ρA):=−Tr⁡(ρA​log⁡ρA)S(A):=S(\rho_{A}):=-\Tr(\rho_{A}\log\rho_{A}). We also write the conditional entropy as S⁡(A|B):=S⁡(A​B)−S⁡(B)S(A|B):=S(AB)-S(B). For a tripartite state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC}, the CMI is

I⁡(A;C|B):=S⁡(A​B)+S⁡(B​C)−S⁡(B)−S⁡(A​B​C).\displaystyle I(A;C|B):=S(AB)+S(BC)-S(B)-S(ABC). (1)

Strong subadditivity asserts I⁡(A;C|B)≥0I(A;C|B)\geq 0 for all ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC}, and the equality case I⁡(A;C|B)=0I(A;C|B)=0 is known to be equivalent to ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} being a quantum Markov state with a specific structural decomposition [12]. Motivated by the classical identity “A−B−CA-B-C is Markov ⇔I⁡(A;C|B)=0\Leftrightarrow I(A;C|B)=0”, we say that A−B−CA-B-C forms a (quantum) Markov chain if I⁡(A;C|B)=0I(A;C|B)=0.

The classical double Markovity phenomenon concerns the simultaneous validity of A−B−CA-B-C and A−C−BA-C-B. In the classical case, this implies the existence of a common random variable JJ that is a function of BB and also a function of CC, such that A−J−(B,C)A-J-(B,C) is Markov. This statement is one of the key devices for converting equality in subadditivity-type inequalities into an independence structure, and hence is tightly intertwined with SDR arguments. In the quantum case, however, the non-commutativity of observables means that one cannot a priori expect a common function of BB and CC in the same sense, and it is unclear what structural statement replaces it. Our first main result provides an exact quantum analogue: we show that “A−B−CA-B-C and A−C−BA-C-B” is equivalent to the existence of compatible projective measurements on BB and CC (equivalently, a common block structure) that induce a classical label JJ for which A−J−(B,C)A-J-(B,C) holds.

A second, equally important, variant of double Markovity appears in SDR-based proofs of entropy power type inequalities, where one works with conditional Markov relations involving an auxiliary variable and requires a full-support assumption to rule out degenerate cases. We establish a quantum counterpart of this conditional double Markovity: for a strictly positive joint state ρA​B​C​D\rho_{ABCD}, the pair of Markov relations A−(B,D)−CA-(B,D)-C and A−(C,D)−BA-(C,D)-B is equivalent to A−D−(B,C)A-D-(B,C). The proof relies on a refinement of the structural decomposition of quantum Markov states, including a uniqueness property of a minimal direct-sum decomposition under full support.

The main contributions of this work are as follows.

  • •

    Quantum double Markovity. For a tripartite state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC}, we characterize the simultaneous Markov conditions A−B−CA-B-C and A−C−BA-C-B in terms of a block-diagonal structure induced by PVMs on BB and CC, and we show that the resulting classical index JJ renders A−J−(B,C)A-J-(B,C) Markov. This is stated precisely in Theorem 1.

  • •

    Conditional quantum double Markovity under full support. For a strictly positive ρA​B​C​D\rho_{ABCD}, we prove that A−(B,D)−CA-(B,D)-C and A−(C,D)−BA-(C,D)-B hold if and only if A−D−(B,C)A-D-(B,C) holds. This is stated in Theorem 2.

To prove the second result, we introduce the minimality of the decomposition introduced in [12].

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we review the SDR paradigm and explain how double Markovity enters equality-case analyses; in particular, we present two classical versions of double Markovity that are most frequently used in the literature. Sections III and IV prove their quantum extensions, establishing Theorems 1 and 2, respectively. We conclude with a brief discussion of implications for extending SDR arguments to quantum information theory.

II The “subadditivity–doubling-rotation” technique and double Markovity

We first recall the classical SDR template and two classical double-Markovity lemmas that will be extended to quantum systems.The idea of the subadditive–doubling rotation technique can be summarized as follows: Let ff be some functional defined on probability distributions. Let f⁡(X)f(X) be a short-hand notation for f⁡(pX)f(p_{X}). Suppose ff has the following properties:

  • •

    (Strict) subadditivity: f⁡(X1,X2)≤f⁡(X1)+f⁡(X2)f(X_{1},X_{2})\leq f(X_{1})+f(X_{2}) with equality if and only if X1⟂X2X_{1}\perp X_{2}, where ⟂\perp is reserved for (classical) independence when discussing classical random variables;

  • •

    Rotation invariant: f⁡(Q​X)=f⁡(X)f(QX)=f(X), where QQ is a unitary matrix. A common running example is X+=12​(X1+X2),X−=12​(X1−X2)X_{+}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(X_{1}+X_{2}),X_{-}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(X_{1}-X_{2}).

  • •

    ff is continuous with respect to weak convergence.

The goal is to maximize f⁡(X)f(X) subject to E⁡[X​XT]⪯KE[XX^{T}]\preceq K. Suppose pX∗p_{X^{*}} is a maximizer for ff with corresponding maximum value vv, then take two independent copies of X∗X^{*}, say X1X_{1} and X2X_{2}.
Note that

2​v\displaystyle 2v =f⁡(X1)+f⁡(X2)=f⁡(X1,X2)\displaystyle=f(X_{1})+f(X_{2})=f(X_{1},X_{2}) (2a)
=f⁡(X+,X−)≤f⁡(X+)+f⁡(X−)≤2​v,\displaystyle=f(X_{+},X_{-})\leq f(X_{+})+f(X_{-})\leq 2v, (2b)

thus, each inequality must have been an equality in the above derivation. Hence, we have X+⟂X−X_{+}\perp X_{-}. Finally, by the Kac-Berstein’s theorem [13],[14], we conclude that X1,X2X_{1},X_{2} are Gaussian distributed.

Double Markovity plays an important role in verifying the strict subadditivity of the functional ff. This is because the “only if” direction of strict subadditivity is often not obvious. The derivation in (2) typically leads only to a certain Markov structure of (X+,X−)(X_{+},X_{-}), rather than directly to their independence.

The following two lemmas, stated with proof, are two classical versions of double Markovity. The first is the standard formulation, while the second is the version used in the proof of the entropy power inequality in [11]. Our main contribution is to provide quantum extensions of both versions.

Lemma 1.

Let A,B,CA,B,C be three (real-valued) random variables defined on the same probability space, such that both the Markov chains A→B→CA\to B\to C and A→C→BA\to C\to B hold. Then

  1. 1.

    There exist functions g1​(B)g_{1}(B) and g2​(C)g_{2}(C) such that g1​(B)=g2​(C)g_{1}(B)=g_{2}(C) with probability one.

  2. 2.

    A→g1​(B)→(B,C)A\to g_{1}(B)\to(B,C) is Markov.

Proof.

Let FA|B=b,FA|C=cF_{A\mid B=b},F_{A\mid C=c} denote the (regular) conditional distributions of AA conditioned on B=bB=b and C=cC=c respectively. We define an equivalence class according to b1≡b2b_{1}\equiv b_{2} if the conditional distributions satisfy FA|B=b1=FA|B=b2F_{A\mid B=b_{1}}=F_{A\mid B=b_{2}}. This defines a partition of ℬ\mathcal{B}. Denote the partitions by ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i}.

Now define g1​(b)g_{1}(b) by b↦ib\mapsto i where b∈ℬib\in\mathcal{B}_{i}. Thus there is a bijection between g1​(b)g_{1}(b) and the conditional distributions FA|B=bF_{A\mid B=b}. Let us similarly define an equivalence class and a partition of the values of CC by 𝒞=⋃j𝒞j\mathcal{C}=\bigcup_{j}\mathcal{C}_{j}.

The Markov chains imply that FA|B,C=FA|BF_{A\mid B,C}=F_{A\mid B} with probability one, and FA|B,C=FA|CF_{A\mid B,C}=F_{A\mid C} with probability one. Therefore we have FA|B=FA|C=FA|B,CF_{A\mid B}=F_{A\mid C}=F_{A\mid B,C} with probability one. On this set define g2​(C)g_{2}(C) to take the same value as g1​(B)g_{1}(B). Clearly, by construction g2​(C)=g1​(B)g_{2}(C)=g_{1}(B) with probability one. Further it is also clear by construction that FA|B,C,g1​(B)=FA|B,C=FA|B=FA|g1​(B)F_{A\mid B,C,g_{1}(B)}=F_{A\mid B,C}=F_{A\mid B}=F_{A\mid g_{1}(B)} with probability one. Thus we also have A→g1​(B)→(B,C)A\to g_{1}(B)\to(B,C) is Markov. ∎

Lemma 2.

Let A,B,C,DA,B,C,D be (real-valued) random variables defined on the same probability space, such that both Markov chains A→(B,D)→CA\to(B,D)\to C and A→(C,D)→BA\to(C,D)\to B hold. Suppose p⁡(a,b,c|d)p(a,b,c|d) has everywhere non-zero density. Then A→D→(B,C)A\to D\to(B,C) forms a Markov chain.

Proof.

Both Markov chains A→(B,D)→CA\to(B,D)\to C and A→(C,D)→BA\to(C,D)\to B yield the relaiton p⁡(a|b,d)=p⁡(a|b,c,d)=p⁡(a|c,d)p(a|b,d)=p(a|b,c,d)=p(a|c,d) for any a,b,c,da,b,c,d, which implies

p⁡(a|b,c,d)=p⁡(a|b,d)\displaystyle p(a|b,c,d)=p(a|b,d)
=\displaystyle= ∑cp⁡(c)​p​(a|b,d)=∑cp⁡(c)​p​(a|c,d)=p⁡(a|d).\displaystyle\sum_{c}p(c)p(a|b,d)=\sum_{c}p(c)p(a|c,d)=p(a|d).

∎

⊗ρC1|(k,l)⊗ρB2,C2|(k,l))\displaystyle\qquad\otimes\rho_{C_{1}|(k,l)}\otimes\rho_{B_{2},C_{2}|(k,l)}\Big)
=\displaystyle= ρA|j⊗(∑k,l:g1​(k)=g2​(l)=jPK,L|J=j(k,l)(ρB1|(k,l)\displaystyle\rho_{A|j}\otimes\Bigg(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k,l:\\ g_{1}(k)=g_{2}(l)=j\end{subarray}}P_{K,L|J=j}(k,l)\,\Big(\rho_{B_{1}|(k,l)}
⊗ρC1|(k,l)⊗ρB2,C2|(k,l))).\displaystyle\qquad\otimes\rho_{C_{1}|(k,l)}\otimes\rho_{B_{2},C_{2}|(k,l)}\Big)\Bigg). (12)

Hence, we conclude that A|j⟂(B1,B2,C1,C2)|jA|j\perp(B_{1},B_{2},C_{1},C_{2})|j, in other words, I⁡(A;B​C|J)=0I(A;BC|J)=0, which implies the condition (ii).

∎

IV Conditional double Markovity for quantum states with full support

Theorem 1 is generalized with the additional system DD as follows when the full support condition is imposed.

Theorem 2.

Let A,B,C,DA,B,C,D be quantum systems with strictly positive joint state ρA​B​C​D\rho_{ABCD}. The following two Markov structures are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    A−(B,D)−CA-(B,D)-C and A−(C,D)−BA-(C,D)-B;

  2. (ii)

    A−D−(B,C)A-D-(B,C).

IV-A Minimal decomposition

The direct-sum/tensor-product decomposition used throughout this paper is the one appearing in the structure theorem for quantum Markov states in [12]. For our purposes, we introduce a minimal version of such a decomposition tailored to a single strictly positive bipartite state ρX​Y\rho_{XY}. In particular, we formulate an explicit minimality criterion and prove a uniqueness property under full support, which will be a key ingredient in the proof of Theorem 2. The system ℋY{\cal H}_{Y} can be decomposed as

ℋY\displaystyle{\cal H}_{Y} =⨁kℋY1|k⊗ℋY2|k.\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{k}{\cal H}_{Y_{1}|k}\otimes{\cal H}_{Y_{2}|k}. (13)

The state ρX​Y\rho_{XY} has the form

ρX​Y\displaystyle\rho_{XY} =⨁kρX,Y1|k⊗ρY2|k\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{k}\rho_{X,Y_{1}|k}\otimes\rho_{Y_{2}|k} (14)

where ρX,Y1|k\rho_{X,Y_{1}|k}, ρY2|k\rho_{Y_{2}|k} are strictly positive matrices on ℋX⊗ℋY1|k{\cal H}_{X}\otimes{\cal H}_{Y_{1}|k} and ℋY2|k{\cal H}_{Y_{2}|k}.

We say that the above decomposition (13) is minimal with respect to XX and ρX​Y\rho_{XY} when the following conditions hold.

  1. (i)

    There is no strict subspace of ℋY1|k{\cal H}_{Y_{1}|k} that can be served as a component of a decomposition.

  2. (ii)

    There is no pair k,k′k,k^{\prime} such that ρX,Y1|k\rho_{X,Y_{1}|k} and ρX,Y1|k′\rho_{X,Y_{1}|k^{\prime}} are related via a unitary transformation.

A minimal decomposition exists because

  1. (i)

    If ρX,Y1|k\rho_{X,Y_{1}|k} can be written as direct sum ⨁lρX,Y1|k,l\bigoplus_{l}\rho_{X,Y_{1}|k,l}, we obtain a refinement by replacing the original block by direct sum of smaller blocks ⊕lρX,Y1|k,l⊗ρY2|k\oplus_{l}\rho_{X,Y_{1}|k,l}\otimes\rho_{Y_{2}|k}.

  2. (ii)

    If there is a pair k,k′k,k^{\prime} in the sense of (2), combining ℋY​2|k{\cal H}_{Y2|k} and ℋY​2|k′{\cal H}_{Y2|k^{\prime}} via direct sum removes such a pair.

In general, a minimal decomposition is not unique. If the support of ρY2|k\rho_{Y_{2}|k} is strictly smaller than ℋY2|k{\cal H}_{Y_{2}|k}, we focus on the kernel ker⁡(ρY2|k)\ker(\rho_{Y_{2}|k}), which is its orthogonal subspace to the support supp⁡(ρY​2|k)\operatorname{supp}(\rho_{Y2|k}) in ℋY​2|k{\cal H}_{Y2|k}.

The subspace ℋY1|k⊗ker⁡(ρY2|k)\mathcal{H}_{Y_{1}|k}\otimes\ker(\rho_{Y_{2}|k}) carries no weight in the state ρX​Y\rho_{XY}, so it could be reassigned to a different block k′k^{\prime}, without harming the decomposition. That is:

ℋY1|k⊗ker⁡(ρY2|k)≅ℋY1|k′⊗ker⁡(ρY2|k)\mathcal{H}_{Y_{1}|k}\otimes\ker(\rho_{Y_{2}|k})\cong\mathcal{H}_{Y_{1}|k^{\prime}}\otimes\ker(\rho_{Y_{2}|k})

for any k′≠kk^{\prime}\neq k, without changing the state. This ambiguity shows that when ρY2|k\rho_{Y_{2}|k} is not full rank, the minimal decomposition is not unique.

In contrast, when the state ρX​Y\rho_{XY} on the joint system X​YXY has full support, there uniquely exists a minimal decomposition with respect to XX and a strictly positive density matrix ρX​Y\rho_{XY}.

Lemma 3.

Let ρX​Y\rho_{XY} be a strictly positive joint state. Suppose ρX​Y\rho_{XY} admits two minimal decompositions:

ℋY\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{Y} =⨁kℋY1|k⊗ℋY2|k,ρX​Y=⨁kρX,Y1|k⊗ρY2|k,\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{k}\mathcal{H}_{Y_{1}|k}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{Y_{2}|k},\quad\rho_{XY}=\bigoplus_{k}\rho_{X,Y_{1}|k}\otimes\rho_{Y_{2}|k}, (15)
ℋY\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{Y} =⨁k′ℋY1|k′′⊗ℋY2|k′′,ρX​Y=⨁k′ρX,Y1|k′′⊗ρY2|k′′.\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{k^{\prime}}\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{Y_{1}|k^{\prime}}\otimes\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{Y_{2}|k^{\prime}},\quad\rho_{XY}=\bigoplus_{k^{\prime}}\rho^{\prime}_{X,Y_{1}|k^{\prime}}\otimes\rho^{\prime}_{Y_{2}|k^{\prime}}. (16)

Then the two decompositions are equivalent up to reordering and unitary equivalence. That is, there exists a bijection ϕ:{k}→{k′}\phi:\{k\}\to\{k^{\prime}\} and unitaries UkU_{k} such that

Uk​ρX,Y1|k⊗ρY2|k​Uk†=ρX,Y1|ϕ⁡(k)′⊗ρY2|ϕ⁡(k)′.U_{k}\rho_{X,Y_{1}|k}\otimes\rho_{Y_{2}|k}U^{\dagger}_{k}=\rho^{\prime}_{X,Y_{1}|\phi(k)}\otimes\rho^{\prime}_{Y_{2}|\phi(k)}.
Proof.

Denote subspaces ℋY1|k⊗ℋY2|k\mathcal{H}_{Y_{1}|k}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{Y_{2}|k} by 𝒱k\mathcal{V}_{k} and ℋY1|k′′⊗ℋY2|k′′\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{Y_{1}|k^{\prime}}\otimes\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{Y_{2}|k^{\prime}} by 𝒱k′′\mathcal{V}^{\prime}_{k^{\prime}}, and let 𝒲k,k′=𝒱k∩𝒱k′′\mathcal{W}_{k,k^{\prime}}=\mathcal{V}_{k}\cap\mathcal{V}^{\prime}_{k^{\prime}}.

Consider a fixed kk, we wish to show that there exists only one 𝒲k,k′\mathcal{W}_{k,k^{\prime}} that is non-trivial and satisfies 𝒱k=𝒲k,k′\mathcal{V}_{k}=\mathcal{W}_{k,k^{\prime}}. Assume the contrast, there are multiple k′k^{\prime}’s, say {k1′,k2′,…,km′}\{k^{\prime}_{1},k^{\prime}_{2},\ldots,k^{\prime}_{m}\}, m≥2m\geq 2, such that 𝒲k,k′\mathcal{W}_{k,k^{\prime}} is non-trivial. Let ρX,Y1|k,k′′\rho^{\prime}_{X,Y_{1}|k,k^{\prime}} denote the state ρX,Y1|k′′\rho^{\prime}_{X,Y_{1}|k^{\prime}} restricted on the space 𝒲k,k′\mathcal{W}_{k,k^{\prime}}. Our assumption yields:

ρX,Y1|k⊗ρY2|k\displaystyle\rho_{X,Y_{1}|k}\otimes\rho_{Y_{2}|k} =⨁i=1mρX,Y1|k,ki′′⊗ρY2|k,ki′′.\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}\rho^{\prime}_{X,Y_{1}|k,k^{\prime}_{i}}\otimes\rho^{\prime}_{Y_{2}|k,k^{\prime}_{i}}.

Since ρX​Y\rho_{XY} is strictly positive, thus ρX,Y1|k,ki′′⊗ρY2|k,ki′′>0\rho^{\prime}_{X,Y_{1}|k,k^{\prime}_{i}}\otimes\rho^{\prime}_{Y_{2}|k,k^{\prime}_{i}}>0 as 𝒲k,ki′\mathcal{W}_{k,k^{\prime}_{i}} is non-trivial subspace. Therefore, we obtain a refinement of the decomposition (15). Contradicting the minimality of the decomposition.

The minimality condition also guarantees that ρX,Y1|k\rho_{X,Y_{1}|k} and ρX,Y1|l\rho_{X,Y_{1}|l} are not unitarily equivalent for k≠lk\neq l. Hence, there must be an one-to-one correspondence ϕ\phi from {k}\{k\} to {k′}\{k^{\prime}\}, and ρX,Y1|k\rho_{X,Y_{1}|k} is unitarily equivalent to ρX,Y1|ϕ⁡(k)′\rho^{\prime}_{X,Y_{1}|\phi(k)}. ∎

IV-B Proof of Theorem 2

Proof.

In the proof, we always choose the HJP direct-sum decomposition to be minimal in the sense of Section IV-A. Since ρA​B​C​D>0\rho_{ABCD}>0, the minimal decomposition with respect to AAA is unique up to permutation and local unitaries. This allows us to identify the decompositions obtained from A−(B,D)−CA-(B,D)-C and from A−(C,D)−BA-(C,D)-B blockwise.

Again, (i​i)⟹(i)(ii)\implies(i) is immediate because I(A;C|B,D)≤I(A;B,C|D)=0I(A;C|B,D)\leq I(A;B,C|D)=0 and I(A;B|C,D)≤I(A;B,C|D)=0I(A;B|C,D)\leq I(A;B,C|D)=0.

Consider the reverse direction. We assume the Markov chains A−(B,D)−CA-(B,D)-C and A−(C,D)−BA-(C,D)-B hold. By applying Theorem 6 of [12] to the Markov chain A−(B,D)−CA-(B,D)-C, ℋB⊗ℋD{\cal H}_{B}\otimes{\cal H}_{D} is decomposed as

ℋB⊗ℋD=⨁kℋB​D1,k⊗ℋB​D2,k.\displaystyle{\cal H}_{B}\otimes{\cal H}_{D}=\bigoplus_{k}{\cal H}_{BD_{1},k}\otimes{\cal H}_{BD_{2},k}. (17)

The state ρA​B​C​D\rho_{ABCD} has the form

ρA​B​C​D\displaystyle\rho_{ABCD} =⨁kρA,B​D1|k⊗ρC,B​D2|k\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{k}\rho_{A,BD_{1}|k}\otimes\rho_{C,BD_{2}|k} (18)

where ρA,B​D1|k\rho_{A,BD_{1}|k}, ρC,B​D2|k\rho_{C,BD_{2}|k} are strictly positive matrices on ℋA⊗ℋB​D1,k{\cal H}_{A}\otimes{\cal H}_{BD_{1},k} and ℋC⊗ℋB​D2,k{\cal H}_{C}\otimes{\cal H}_{BD_{2},k}.

Since the minimality condition with respect to AA and ρA​B​C​D\rho_{ABCD} is decided by the structures of ℋB​D​1,k{\cal H}_{BD1,k}, when the decomposition (17) is minimal with respect to AA and ρA​B​D\rho_{ABD}, the decomposition

ℋB⊗ℋC⊗ℋD=⨁kℋB​D1,k⊗ℋC⊗ℋB​D2,k\displaystyle{\cal H}_{B}\otimes{\cal H}_{C}\otimes{\cal H}_{D}=\bigoplus_{k}{\cal H}_{BD_{1},k}\otimes{\cal H}_{C}\otimes{\cal H}_{BD_{2},k} (19)

is minimal with respect to AA and ρA​B​C​D\rho_{ABCD}. Now, we assume that the decomposition (17) is minimal with respect to AA and ρA​B​D\rho_{ABD}.

Next, similarly, by applying Theorem 6 of [12] to the Markov chain A−(C,D)−BA-(C,D)-B, ℋC⊗ℋD{\cal H}_{C}\otimes{\cal H}_{D} is decomposed as

ℋC⊗ℋD=⨁lℋC​D1,l⊗ℋC​D2,l.\displaystyle{\cal H}_{C}\otimes{\cal H}_{D}=\bigoplus_{l}{\cal H}_{CD_{1},l}\otimes{\cal H}_{CD_{2},l}. (20)

The state ρA​B​C​D\rho_{ABCD} has the form

ρA​B​C​D\displaystyle\rho_{ABCD} =⨁lρA,C​D1|l⊗ρB,C​D2|l\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{l}\rho_{A,CD_{1}|l}\otimes\rho_{B,CD_{2}|l} (21)

where ρA,C​D1|l\rho_{A,CD_{1}|l}, ρB,C​D2|l\rho_{B,CD_{2}|l} are strictly positive matrices on ℋA⊗ℋC​D1,l{\cal H}_{A}\otimes{\cal H}_{CD_{1},l} and ℋB⊗ℋC​D2,l{\cal H}_{B}\otimes{\cal H}_{CD_{2},l}. Also, we assume that the decomposition (20) is minimal with respect to AA and ρA​C​D\rho_{ACD}. Hence,

ℋB⊗ℋC⊗ℋD=⨁lℋC​D1,l⊗ℋB⊗ℋC​D2,l\displaystyle{\cal H}_{B}\otimes{\cal H}_{C}\otimes{\cal H}_{D}=\bigoplus_{l}{\cal H}_{CD_{1},l}\otimes{\cal H}_{B}\otimes{\cal H}_{CD_{2},l} (22)

is also minimal with respect to AA and ρA​B​C​D\rho_{ABCD}. Since ρA​B​C​D\rho_{ABCD} is a strictly positive density matrix, the uniqueness of the minimal decomposition with respect to AA and ρA​B​C​D\rho_{ABCD} guarantee the one-to-one map k↦l⁡(k)k\mapsto l(k) such that

ℋB​D1,k=ℋC​D1,l⁡(k),ℋC⊗ℋB​D2,k=ℋB⊗ℋC​D2,l⁡(k),\displaystyle{\cal H}_{BD_{1},k}={\cal H}_{CD_{1},l(k)},\quad{\cal H}_{C}\otimes{\cal H}_{BD_{2},k}={\cal H}_{B}\otimes{\cal H}_{CD_{2},l(k)},

with

ρA,B​D1|k=ρA,C​D1|l⁡(k),ρC,B​D2|k=ρB,C​D2|l⁡(k).\displaystyle\rho_{A,BD_{1}|k}=\rho_{A,CD_{1}|l(k)},\quad\rho_{C,BD_{2}|k}=\rho_{B,CD_{2}|l(k)}.

Therefore, for each kk, there exists a subspace 𝒦D1,k⊗𝒦D2,k⊂ℋD{\cal K}_{D_{1},k}\otimes{\cal K}_{D_{2},k}\subset{\cal H}_{D} such that ℋC⊗ℋB​D2,k=ℋB⊗ℋC​D2,l⁡(k){\cal H}_{C}\otimes{\cal H}_{BD_{2},k}={\cal H}_{B}\otimes{\cal H}_{CD_{2},l(k)} restricted on ℋD\mathcal{H}_{D} gives 𝒦D2,k{\cal K}_{D_{2},k} and ℋB​D1,k=ℋC​D1,l⁡(k){\cal H}_{BD_{1},k}={\cal H}_{CD_{1},l(k)} restricted on ℋD\mathcal{H}_{D} gives 𝒦D1,k{\cal K}_{D_{1},k}. Since the kk-th subspace of decomposition (19) can be written as

ℋB​D1,k⊗ℋC⊗ℋB​D2,k\displaystyle{\cal H}_{BD_{1},k}\otimes{\cal H}_{C}\otimes{\cal H}_{BD_{2},k} =ℋB​D1,k⊗ℋB⊗ℋC​D2,l⁡(k),\displaystyle={\cal H}_{BD_{1},k}\otimes{\cal H}_{B}\otimes{\cal H}_{CD_{2},l(k)},

yielding ℋC⊗ℋB​D2,k{\cal H}_{C}\otimes{\cal H}_{BD_{2},k} carries the whole ℋB⊗ℋC\mathcal{H}_{B}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{C}, while ℋB​D1,k\mathcal{H}_{BD_{1},k} does contain any part of ℋB\mathcal{H}_{B}, i.e., ℋB​D1,k=𝒦D1,k\mathcal{H}_{BD_{1},k}=\mathcal{K}_{D_{1},k}.

Therefore, the space ℋD{\cal H}_{D} is decomposed as

ℋD=⊕k𝒦D​1,k⊗𝒦D​2,k.\displaystyle{\cal H}_{D}=\oplus_{k}{\cal K}_{D1,k}\otimes{\cal K}_{D2,k}. (23)

the state ρA,B​D1|k=ρA,C​D1|l⁡(k)\rho_{A,BD_{1}|k}=\rho_{A,CD_{1}|l(k)} can be written as a state ρA,D1|k\rho_{A,D_{1}|k} on ℋA⊗𝒦D1,k{\cal H}_{A}\otimes{\cal K}_{D_{1},k}, and ρC,B​D2|k=ρB,C​D2|l⁡(k)\rho_{C,BD_{2}|k}=\rho_{B,CD_{2}|l(k)} can written as a state ρB​C,D2|k\rho_{BC,D_{2}|k} on ℋB⊗ℋC⊗𝒦D2,k{\cal H}_{B}\otimes{\cal H}_{C}\otimes{\cal K}_{D_{2},k}. Hence, the state ρA​B​C​D\rho_{ABCD} has the block form

ρA​B​C​D=⊕kρA,D1|k⊗ρB​C,D2|k,\displaystyle\rho_{ABCD}=\oplus_{k}\rho_{A,D_{1}|k}\otimes\rho_{BC,D_{2}|k}, (24)

which implies the Markov chain A−D−(B,C)A-D-(B,C). ∎

V Conclusion

In this paper, we have established quantum versions of the double Markovity phenomenon and have provided two structural characterizations that parallel the most commonly used classical formulations. First, for a tripartite state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC}, we have shown that the simultaneous Markov conditions A−B−CA\!-\!B\!-\!C and A−C−BA\!-\!C\!-\!B are equivalent to the existence of projective measurements on BB and CC that induce a common classical label JJ and render A−J−(B,C)A\!-\!J\!-\!(B,C) a Markov chain (Theorem 1). This characterization has identified an explicitly classical piece of information—the index JJ—that captures the part of BB and CC relevant to screening off AA, thereby providing a faithful quantum analogue of the classical “common summary variable” picture.

Second, under a full-support (strictly positive) assumption, we have established a conditional double Markovity statement for four-party states: for ρA​B​C​D>0\rho_{ABCD}>0, the pair of Markov relations A−(B,D)−CA\!-\!(B,D)\!-\!C and A−(C,D)−BA\!-\!(C,D)\!-\!B has been shown to be equivalent to A−D−(B,C)A\!-\!D\!-\!(B,C) (Theorem 2). The proof has relied on a refined use of the structural decomposition of quantum Markov states, together with a uniqueness property of a minimal direct-sum decomposition under full support.

Taken together, these results have removed a key bottleneck in extending the subadditivity–doubling–rotation methodology to quantum settings. In particular, they have supplied the missing equality-case mechanism that is frequently required when strict subadditivity is invoked in SDR-type arguments. We expect that the present structural theorems will serve as a reusable tool in future work on quantum Gaussian extremality and related information inequalities, where one needs to convert Markov-type conclusions into explicit structural constraints on quantum states.
